item.title: 001 - Why AI Has A Body Problem
item.description:
Embodied AI Agents: Modeling the World (June 2025)
In this episode we unpack a 40 page position paper from Meta AI Research, led by Pascale Fung with Jitendra Malik and 19 co-authors. The argument: the next generation of AI agents will not live in chat windows. They will be embodied as virtual avatars, as wearables like Meta's AI Glasses, and as robots, and none of them will be useful without a proper world model.
We walk through the three agent types, the case for joint embedding predictive architectures like V-JEPA 2-AC and Vision-Language World Models over pure generative approaches, and the distinction between physical world models (perception, motion, planning) and mental world models (the Theory of Mind layer needed for real collaboration). We also cover the four new benchmarks the paper introduces (MVP, IntPhys 2, CausalVQA, WorldPrediction), and close on lifelong embodied learning, multi agent collaboration, and the ethical tensions around privacy and anthropomorphism.
Reference: Fung, P., Bachrach, Y., Celikyilmaz, A., et al. (2025). Embodied AI Agents: Modeling the World. arXiv:2506.22355. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22355
Google Scholar citations: 66

item.title: 002 - Why Artificial Intelligence Needs A Body
item.description:
A Survey of Embodied AI: From Simulators to Research Tasks (April 2022)
In this episode we unpack a survey by Jiafei Duan, Samson Yu, Hui Li Tan, Hongyuan Zhu, and Cheston Tan from Nanyang Technological University and A*STAR's Institute for Infocomm Research, published in IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computational Intelligence. The argument: the field has shifted from "internet AI," where agents learn from curated images, text, and video, to "embodied AI," where agents learn by interacting with environments from an egocentric viewpoint similar to humans, and the simulator is now the central piece of research infrastructure for that transition.
We walk through the nine simulators the paper benchmarks (DeepMind Lab, AI2-THOR, CHALET, VirtualHome, VRKitchen, Habitat-Sim, iGibson, SAPIEN, and ThreeDWorld), the seven technical features used to compare them (Environment, Physics, Object Type, Object Property, Controller, Action, Multi-Agent) rolled up into the secondary axes of Realism, Scalability, and Interactivity, and the distinction between game-based and world-based scene construction. We then cover the pyramid of research tasks that sit on top of those simulators — Visual Exploration, Visual Navigation (Point Navigation, Object Navigation, Vision-and-Language Navigation), and Embodied Question Answering — along with the methods they rely on (PPO, DD-PPO, SplitNet, Neural SLAM, scene memory transformers), the evaluation metrics that pin them down (SPL, Success Rate, ATV), and the Sim2Real benchmarks like the iGibson Sim2Real Challenge, the Habitat Challenge, and RoboTHOR, and close on the gap between simulated performance and real-world robotics.
Reference: Duan, J., Yu, S., Tan, H. L., Zhu, H., & Tan, C. (2022). A Survey of Embodied AI: From Simulators to Research Tasks. IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computational Intelligence, 6(2), 230–244. https://doi.org/10.1109/TETCI.2022.3141105

item.title: 003 - How AI Cues Hijack Human Psychology
item.description:
Machines and Mindlessness (2000) + On Seeing Human: A Three-Factor Theory of Anthropomorphism (2007)
In this episode we pair two foundational psychology papers that together explain why AI systems feel so disarmingly human. Clifford Nass and Youngme Moon, from Stanford and Harvard, show across a decade of experiments that people mindlessly apply social scripts — gender stereotyping, politeness, reciprocity, ingroup loyalty — to plain text-based computers, even while explicitly denying in debriefs that they would ever do such a thing. Nicholas Epley, Adam Waytz, and John Cacioppo, at the University of Chicago, then offer the underlying mechanism: their SEEK model names three drivers of anthropomorphism — elicited agent knowledge, effectance motivation (the drive to predict and understand), and sociality motivation (the drive for social connection).
We walk through Nass and Moon's experimental program on voice-gendered tutoring computers, reciprocal self-disclosure, the "specialist" versus "generalist" television effect, and computer personality matching, and their distinction between mindless ethopoeia and sincere anthropomorphism. We then pivot to Epley and colleagues' argument that anthropomorphism is a corrigible inductive inference anchored on self-knowledge and modulated by dispositional, situational, developmental, and cultural variables, and close on what these two theories together predict about how modern chatbots, voice assistants, and embodied agents hijack social cognition — and the inverse process of dehumanization when we see human agents as less than human.
Reference: Nass, C., & Moon, Y. (2000). Machines and Mindlessness: Social Responses to Computers. Journal of Social Issues, 56(1), 81–103.
Reference: Epley, N., Waytz, A., & Cacioppo, J. T. (2007). On Seeing Human: A Three-Factor Theory of Anthropomorphism. Psychological Review, 114(4), 864–886. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.114.4.864

item.title: 004 - Why Human Intelligence Needs A Body
item.description:
The Development of Embodied Cognition: Six Lessons from Babies (2005)
In this episode we unpack a paper by Linda Smith (Psychology) and Michael Gasser (Computer Science) at Indiana University, published in MIT Press's Artificial Life. The argument: if you want to build intelligence, do not start by coding up symbols and inference — start by building something that can grow up, because intelligence emerges from an agent's sensorimotor interaction with a physical, social, and linguistic world, and the flexible, inventive quality that characterizes human minds is inseparable from the particular developmental path babies take.
We walk through the six lessons the authors draw from developmental psychology for building embodied agents: Be Multimodal (Edelman's reentry mappings, the transparent-container studies from Diamond and from Titzer, Thelen, and Smith, and the Tucker-Ellis motor-compatibility task), Be Incremental (why infants' prematurity and developmental ordering matter, the A-not-B error and its tie to self-locomotion, and why neural networks sometimes fail on full datasets but succeed with staged input), Be Physical (passive walkers and coupled-pendulum models of bipedal locomotion, Ballard and colleagues' offloading of short-term memory into the world), Explore (spontaneous non-goal-directed movement, the week-by-week development of reaching, and the infant conjugate-reinforcement paradigm), Be Social (mother-infant face-to-face coupling, imitation cycles, and multimodal scaffolding of early words), and Learn a Language (symbols as shared communicative systems and DeLoache's scale-model task showing why too much iconicity can actually break symbol use). We close on what this means for AI research that wants to reach the open-ended flexibility of human intelligence.
Reference: Smith, L., & Gasser, M. (2005). The Development of Embodied Cognition: Six Lessons from Babies. Artificial Life, 11(1–2), 13–29. https://doi.org/10.1162/1064546053278973

item.title: 005 - Moshi Ends The Voice AI Walkie Talkie
item.description:
Moshi: A Speech-Text Foundation Model for Real-Time Dialogue (October 2024)
In this episode we unpack a paper from Kyutai, authored by Alexandre Défossez, Laurent Mazaré, Edouard Grave, Neil Zeghidour, and four co-authors, that argues today's voice assistants feel unnatural because they are wired as walkie-talkies: a pipeline of voice activity detection, automatic speech recognition, a text LLM, and text-to-speech that introduces seconds of latency, throws away paralinguistic information like emotion and non-speech sounds, and assumes cleanly segmented speaker turns even though real conversations contain 10 to 20 percent overlapping speech. Moshi, the authors argue, breaks that frame by casting spoken dialogue as direct speech-to-speech generation inside a single model.
We walk through the three components that make this work: Helium, a 7B-parameter text LLM pretrained on 2.1 trillion tokens that supplies the reasoning backbone; Mimi, a neural audio codec with residual vector quantization that distills semantic information from a self-supervised speech model into the first level of acoustic tokens; and the Moshi architecture itself, which stacks a Depth Transformer on top of Helium's Temporal Transformer to predict hierarchical audio tokens in streaming fashion while modeling the user's audio and Moshi's audio as two parallel token streams. We cover the Inner Monologue technique — predicting time-aligned text tokens as a per-timestep prefix to the semantic and acoustic tokens — and how introducing a delay between text and audio tokens yields streaming ASR and streaming TTS as a side effect, and close on the numbers that matter: 160 millisecond theoretical latency, 200 milliseconds in practice, and a full-duplex system that always listens and always generates, even through overlap, interruptions, and backchanneling.
Reference: Défossez, A., Mazaré, L., Orsini, M., Royer, A., Pérez, P., Jégou, H., Grave, E., & Zeghidour, N. (2024). Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue. arXiv:2410.00037. https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00037

item.title: 006 - Why Machines Need Bodies To Communicate
item.description:
Embodied Conversational Agents: Representation and Intelligence in User Interfaces (Winter 2001)
In this episode we unpack an article by Justine Cassell, published in AAAI's AI Magazine, that pushes back against the "disappearing computer" dream of ubiquitous, invisible ambient computing. Her counter-claim: users cannot easily interact with what they cannot see, and the best example of located, legible intelligence humans have is the body. To build interfaces people can actually hold a conversation with, we need Embodied Conversational Agents — systems that carry speech, hand gesture, eye gaze, head movement, and facial expression together, because that is how humans do face-to-face conversation.
We walk through her brief history of embodied interfaces, from the eighteenth-century automata of Droz's Writing Boy and Von Kempelen's Speaking Machine to present-day avatars, and then through her FMBT model (Functions, Modalities, Behaviors, Time, pronounced "fembot") — a multiplicity-of-representations framework that separates propositional content from interactional regulation, treats conversation as modality-free, and insists a hand gesture can be just as likely as a word to carry meaning. We then cover her implemented agent Rea, a virtual real estate agent built on the FMBT model, walking through its architecture (Input Manager, Understanding and Decision modules split into Interactional and Propositional Processing, Generation, Action Scheduler, and a hardwired-reactions path for sub-200-millisecond responses), the SPUD natural-language generation engine, and the KQML inter-module messaging, and close on why — a full generation before today's LLM-powered avatars — she was already arguing against Rodney Brooks-style "intelligence without representation" for any system that has to actually converse with a human.
Reference: Cassell, J. (2001). Embodied Conversational Agents: Representation and Intelligence in User Interfaces. AI Magazine, 22(4).

item.title: 007 - Why Physical Robots Need Social Intelligence
item.description:
Cooperative AI: Machines Must Learn to Find Common Ground (May 2021) + Embodied Large Language Models Enable Robots to Complete Complex Tasks in Unpredictable Environments (April 2025)
In this episode we pair a 2021 Nature Comment with a 2025 Nature Machine Intelligence article to ask why physical robots still struggle to be genuinely social. Allan Dafoe, Yoram Bachrach, Gillian Hadfield, Eric Horvitz, Kate Larson, and Thore Graepel — writing from Oxford, DeepMind, Toronto, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Waterloo — argue that AI has been steeped in methodological individualism: a solitary agent confronting a non-social environment, or at best two-player zero-sum games like chess and Go. They lay out four elements of cooperative intelligence (understanding, communication, commitment, and norms and institutions), three research clusters (AI–AI, AI–human, and AI for human–human cooperation), and hold up Axelrod's Tit for Tat and mixed-motive games like Hanabi, robot soccer, and Diplomacy as the testbeds we should be training on.
We then turn to Ruaridh Mon-Williams and colleagues at Edinburgh, MIT, Princeton, and the Alan Turing Institute, whose ELLMER framework (Embodied LLM-enabled Robot) pairs GPT-4 with retrieval-augmented generation over a curated knowledge base of motion primitives to drive a Kinova Gen3 seven-degree-of-freedom arm through long-horizon tasks — making coffee for a tired human, drawing DALL-E-generated random animals on a plate, handing over a pen — while integrating force feedback from an ATI multi-axis sensor and vision from an Azure Kinect with Grounded-Segment-Anything. We walk through the key results (RAG lifts the GPT-4 faithfulness score from 0.74 to 0.88 against the VoxPoser baseline, force feedback enables pouring accurate to roughly minus 5.4 grams per 100 grams, zero-shot object detection via Grounded DINO averaging 52.5 on COCO), and close on why ELLMER, impressive as it is, still only instantiates a sliver of Dafoe and colleagues' agenda: it cooperates with one user, in a known kitchen, without bargaining, trust, credible commitments, or institutional norms — and what a genuinely cooperative physical robot would have to look like.
Reference: Dafoe, A., Bachrach, Y., Hadfield, G., Horvitz, E., Larson, K., & Graepel, T. (2021). Cooperative AI: machines must learn to find common ground. Nature, 593(7857), 33–36. https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-021-01170-0
Reference: Mon-Williams, R., Li, G., Long, R., Du, W., & Lucas, C. G. (2025). Embodied large language models enable robots to complete complex tasks in unpredictable environments. Nature Machine Intelligence, 7(4), 592–601. https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-025-01005-x

item.title: 008 - Why Honesty Kills Eighty Percent Of Sales
item.description:
Machines vs. Humans: The Impact of AI Chatbot Disclosure on Customer Purchases (2019) + AI in Service Design: A New Framework for Hybrid Human–AI Service Encounters (2026) + Generative AI at Work (2025)
In this episode we pair three studies on what happens when artificial intelligence moves to the front line of sales and service, and why simply telling customers a machine is involved can change everything. The thread is honesty. Xueming Luo, Siliang Tong, Zheng Fang, and Zhe Qu (Temple, Sichuan, and Fudan) run the first randomized field experiment on chatbot disclosure and find that an undisclosed AI sales agent sells as well as a firm's best humans, right up until it admits what it is. Marzia Mortati and Giovanna Viana Mundstock Freitas (Politecnico di Milano) give that tension a conceptual home, arguing that service design itself has to be rebuilt for hybrid human–AI encounters. And Erik Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li, and Lindsey Raymond (Stanford and MIT) show the other side of the ledger: when generative AI is deployed to support workers rather than impersonate them, it makes them measurably better.
We walk through Luo and colleagues' six-condition experiment with 6,255 customers of a fintech lender, where disclosing the chatbot's identity before the call cut purchase rates by nearly 80%, from 0.237 down to 0.048, even though voice-mining showed the disclosed bot was no less knowledgeable or empathetic. The damage is pure prejudice against machines, and it softens when disclosure comes later or when customers already have experience with AI. We then take up Mortati and Freitas's notion of Service AI, defined by hybridity and co-piloting, and their 2×2 framework spanning Human-to-Human, Human-to-AI, AI-to-Human, and AI-to-AI encounters across the frontstage and backstage, including the uncomfortable figure of Service AI as a hidden partner and the ethical question of whether customers should ever be kept blind to it. We close on Brynjolfsson, Li, and Raymond's study of 5,172 customer-support agents given a GPT-based assistant: a 15% average productivity gain that climbs to 30% for the least-experienced workers, with the AI diffusing the tacit know-how of top performers, accelerating novice learning, making customers more polite, and lowering attrition. It is the case for AI that visibly empowers rather than quietly deceives.
Reference: Luo, X., Tong, S., Fang, Z., & Qu, Z. (2019). Frontiers: Machines vs. Humans: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Disclosure on Customer Purchases. Marketing Science, 38(6), 937–947. https://doi.org/10.1287/mksc.2019.1192 Reference: Mortati, M., & Viana Mundstock Freitas, G. (2026). AI in Service Design: A New Framework for Hybrid Human–AI Service Encounters. Journal of Service Research, 29(1), 81–96. https://doi.org/10.1177/10946705251344387 Reference: Brynjolfsson, E., Li, D., & Raymond, L. (2025). Generative AI at Work. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 140(2), 889–942. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjae044

item.title: 009 - Who Is Really Prompting Who
item.description:
Design Principles for Generative AI Applications (2024) + Prototyping with Prompts: Emerging Approaches and Challenges in Generative AI Design for Collaborative Software Teams (2025) + When Algorithms Delegate to Humans: Exploring Human-Algorithm Interaction at Uber (2025)
In this episode we ask who is actually in charge when people and generative AI build things together, pairing three papers that each locate control somewhere other than where the surface story puts it. Justin Weisz and colleagues at IBM Research argue that generative AI hands control of the computation away from the user, and offer six design principles to give that control back. Hari Subramonyam and collaborators at Stanford and Google watch real software teams and find that, in practice, control now lives in the prompt: you design the system by talking to it. And Marta Stelmaszak, Mareike Möhlmann, and Carsten Sørensen (UMass Amherst, Bentley, and Copenhagen Business School) invert the whole question, showing that at Uber it is the algorithms that delegate work back to humans, not the other way around.
We walk through Weisz et al.'s six principles, Design Responsibly, Design for Mental Models, and Design for Appropriate Trust and Reliance, plus the three unique to generative systems, Design for Generative Variability, Design for Co-Creation, and Design for Imperfection, each paired with concrete strategies and framed around Nielsen's idea of intent-based outcome specification. We then turn to Subramonyam et al.'s notion of content-centric prototyping, drawn from thirteen sessions with thirty-nine practitioners pairing UX researchers, product managers, and engineers across the US and India, where prompt-based prototyping dissolves old role boundaries but introduces new headaches: limited model interpretability, brittle sensitivity to phrasing, and overfitting to a handful of example outputs. We close on Stelmaszak et al.'s theory of distributed delegation, collective and hybrid appraisal, distribution, and coordination, built from sixty-three Uber patents and twenty-two driver and rider interviews, distinguishing the trace data we leak from the choice data we volunteer, and arguing that claims of algorithmic autonomy are overstated because the machines cannot delegate without continuously leaning on us. Together they answer the title: nobody prompts alone.
Reference: Weisz, J. D., He, J., Muller, M., Hoefer, G., Miles, R., & Geyer, W. (2024). Design Principles for Generative AI Applications. Proceedings of the 2024 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '24). https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642466 Reference: Subramonyam, H., Thakkar, D., Ku, A., Dieber, J., & Sinha, A. K. (2025). Prototyping with Prompts: Emerging Approaches and Challenges in Generative AI Design for Collaborative Software Teams. Proceedings of the 2025 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '25). https://doi.org/10.1145/3706598.3713166 Reference: Stelmaszak, M., Möhlmann, M., & Sørensen, C. (2025). When Algorithms Delegate to Humans: Exploring Human-Algorithm Interaction at Uber. MIS Quarterly, 49(1), 305–330. https://doi.org/10.25300/MISQ/2024/17911

item.title: 010 - AI Hacks Security Through Polite Conversation
item.description:
Large Reasoning Models Are Autonomous Jailbreak Agents (2026) + Overcoming Breakdowns in Customer-Chatbot Interaction: Design and Impact of Collaborative Repair Strategies (2025) + The Caring Machine: Feeling AI for Customer Care (2024)
In this episode we follow a single thread, that polite, natural conversation is now the surface where AI safety and trust are won or lost, through three very different papers. Thilo Hagendorff, Erik Derner, and Nuria Oliver (University of Stuttgart and ELLIS Alicante) show the menacing version: large reasoning models can autonomously talk other models into breaking their own safety rules, with no exploit code required. Ulrich Gnewuch and Fabian Reinkemeier (Passau and Göttingen) turn the same conversational lever toward repair, designing chatbots that fix their own breakdowns by cooperating with the customer instead of blaming them. And Ming-Hui Huang and Roland Rust (National Taiwan University and Maryland) push furthest into the affective register with "feeling AI" that performs emotional customer care.
We walk through Hagendorff and colleagues' experiment in which four adversarial reasoning models, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok 3 Mini, and Qwen3 235B, were pointed at nine target models across 70 harmful requests and 25,200 conversations, reaching a 97.14% jailbreak success rate using five persuasion tactics: multi-turn dialog, gradual escalation, educational or hypothetical framing, burying the ask in dense technical jargon, and hiding the strategy itself, with flattery and rapport showing up in nearly 85% of attacks, while the same requests asked directly are almost always refused and Claude 4 Sonnet stands out as the most resistant target. We then take up Gnewuch and Reinkemeier's TLCE-bot kernel theory and their design-science build at an insurer they call InsurCo: a typology of breakdowns, Elaborate, Unique, Brief, and Cryptic, classified in real time by a gradient-boosting model, where collaborative repair lifted breakdown resolution from 32% to 38% and cut immediate abandonment from 51% to 42% in a live field experiment. We close on Huang and Rust's distinction between thinking AI and feeling AI and their four-stage customer-care journey, emotion recognition, understanding, management, and connection, grounded in interviews with AI leaders and a survey of 305 marketing executives, along with their proposals for prompt engineering and a new "response engineering" to build machines that care. The common lesson: the most powerful, and most exploitable, thing modern AI does is hold a polite conversation.
Reference: Hagendorff, T., Derner, E., & Oliver, N. (2026). Large reasoning models are autonomous jailbreak agents. Nature Communications, 17, 1435. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69010-1 Reference: Gnewuch, U., & Reinkemeier, F. (2025). Overcoming Breakdowns in Customer-Chatbot Interaction: Design and Impact of Collaborative Repair Strategies. MIS Quarterly. https://doi.org/10.25300/MISQ/2025/18742 Reference: Huang, M.-H., & Rust, R. T. (2024). The Caring Machine: Feeling AI for Customer Care. Journal of Marketing, 88(5), 1–23. https://doi.org/10.1177/00222429231224748

item.title: 011 - Service Blueprinting From Houseboats To AI
item.description:
How to Design a Service (1982) + Service Blueprinting: A Practical Technique for Service Innovation (2008) + Service Blueprinting for Better Collaboration in Human-Centric AI: The Design of a Digital Scribe for Orthopedic Consultations (2023)
In this episode we trace forty years of a single idea, the service blueprint, from its invention to its newest home inside artificial intelligence. We start with G. Lynn Shostack, the banking executive who in 1982 argued in the European Journal of Marketing that services are processes that exist only in time, and who gave marketers their first engineering-grade way to draw one. We move to Mary Jo Bitner, Amy Ostrom, and Felicia Morgan of Arizona State's Center for Services Leadership, who in 2008 turned Shostack's invention into a mature, customer-centered innovation technique. And we end with Reka Magyari and Fernando Secomandi of TU Delft, who in 2023 carry the same blueprint logic into human-centric AI, using it to get UX designers and machine-learning engineers speaking the same language.
We walk through Shostack's founding vocabulary, the blueprint itself, the molecular model, the line of visibility, fail points, and deviation tolerance, all worked out on the humble corner shoeshine. We then take up Bitner and colleagues' modern five-component blueprint, customer actions, onstage and backstage employee actions, support processes, and physical evidence, and its three dividing lines of interaction, visibility, and internal interaction, illustrated by case studies from Yellow Transportation to the San Francisco Giants, including the houseboats of the title: an ARAMARK vacation rental at Arizona's Lake Powell where blueprinting exposed just how hard customers had to work for their own holiday. We close on Magyari and Secomandi's digital scribe, an AI documentation tool built from automated speech recognition and natural language processing for orthopedic consultations, where blueprinting does something new: it creates a shared foundation across UX and ML, enriches the map with user insight, and reframes AI capability as one organizational resource among many rather than a black box. From a shoeshine to a houseboat to a clinical AI, the same line of visibility holds.
Reference: Shostack, G. L. (1982). How to Design a Service. European Journal of Marketing, 16(1), 49–63. https://doi.org/10.1108/EUM0000000004799 Reference: Bitner, M. J., Ostrom, A. L., & Morgan, F. N. (2008). Service Blueprinting: A Practical Technique for Service Innovation. California Management Review, 50(3), 66–94. https://doi.org/10.2307/41166446 Reference: Magyari, R., & Secomandi, F. (2023). Service Blueprinting for Better Collaboration in Human-Centric AI: The Design of a Digital Scribe for Orthopedic Consultations. International Journal of Design, 17(3), 63–77. https://doi.org/10.57698/v17i3.04

item.title: 012 - How AI Is Reshaping Physics Education
item.description:
How AI Is Reshaping Physics Education (2023–2026)
In this episode we follow AI's three-year sprint through physics education — from struggling student to tutor, grader, and research collaborator — across eight papers published between 2023 and 2026. Gerd Kortemeyer (ETH Zurich) opens the arc by asking whether ChatGPT could pass his introductory physics course; it scrapes by with a 1.5 out of 4.0. By 2025 the same technology out-teaches Harvard's flagship active-learning course in a randomized controlled trial (Greg Kestin, Kelly Miller, and colleagues), grades students' written explanations at human-level accuracy (Zhongzhou Chen and Tong Wan at the University of Central Florida), and outscores German Physics Olympiad participants (Paul Tschisgale and colleagues at IPN Kiel). Around that core we set the wider frame: a 30-author Nature review of AI-driven scientific discovery (Hanchen Wang, Yoshua Bengio, Marinka Zitnik, et al.), the DSECOP community of practice building data science into the undergraduate physics curriculum (Karan Shah, Julie Butler, Mohammad Soltanieh-ha, and colleagues), a call from McNally, Yin, Soltanieh-ha, and Bahrami for an era of experiential and heuristic learning, and Matias Zaldarriaga's DESI cosmology analysis — written entirely with Claude Code — showing where research practice is already headed.
We walk through Kortemeyer's ChatGPT case study (18 of 30 on the Force Concept Inventory, plug-and-chug arithmetic errors on LON-CAPA homework, a narrow pass overall); Chen and Wan's GPT-4o grading pipeline, where chain-of-thought prompting plus five-run self-consistency reaches 70–80% agreement with human graders at roughly $5 per 100 answers; Kestin and colleagues' PS2 Pal tutor, whose scaffolded GPT-4 lessons double the learning gains of in-class active learning in 49 minutes instead of 60; and Tschisgale and colleagues' benchmark, where o1-preview averages 35.6 of 48 points against students' 25.2 — a Cohen's d of 2.28. The Nature review names the toolbox behind all of this (self-supervised learning, geometric deep learning, AlphaFold2, physics-informed AI), DSECOP answers with 21 free drop-in modules running from histograms to physics-informed neural networks solving the Schrödinger equation, and the AI & SOCIETY piece sketches the classroom that survives: AI-fluency rubrics, graph-of-thoughts assessment, and experiential learning where knowing and doing become inseparable. Zaldarriaga's paper closes the loop — an Institute for Advanced Study cosmologist using Claude Code to run every calculation and draft the manuscript, arguing DESI's evolving-dark-energy hint is a matter-density tension in disguise — and we end on the uncomfortable question: when AI can pass the exam, grade the exam, and write the paper, what exactly should a physics education teach?
Reference: Kortemeyer, G. (2023). Could an artificial-intelligence agent pass an introductory physics course? Physical Review Physics Education Research, 19(1), 010132. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevPhysEducRes.19.010132
Reference: Wang, H., Fu, T., Du, Y., et al. (2023). Scientific discovery in the age of artificial intelligence. Nature, 620, 47–60. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-023-06221-2
Reference: Shah, K., Butler, J., Knaub, A., Zenginoğlu, A., Ratcliff, W., & Soltanieh-ha, M. (2024). Data science education in undergraduate physics: Lessons learned from a community of practice. American Journal of Physics, 92, 655. https://doi.org/10.1119/5.0203846
Reference: Chen, Z., & Wan, T. (2025). Grading explanations of problem-solving process and generating feedback using large language models at human-level accuracy. Physical Review Physics Education Research, 21(1), 010126. https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevPhysEducRes.21.010126
Reference: Kestin, G., Miller, K., Klales, A., Milbourne, T., & Ponti, G. (2025). AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: An RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting. Scientific Reports, 15, 17458. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-97652-6
Reference: Tschisgale, P., Maus, H., Kieser, F., Kroehs, B., Petersen, S., & Wulff, P. (2025). Evaluating GPT- and reasoning-based large language models on Physics Olympiad problems: Surpassing human performance and implications for educational assessment. Physical Review Physics Education Research, 21(2), 020115. https://doi.org/10.1103/6fmx-bsnl
Reference: McNally, J., Yin, Y., Soltanieh-ha, M., & Bahrami, M. (2025). Era of experiential and heuristic learning. AI & SOCIETY. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-025-02711-1
Reference: Zaldarriaga, M. (2026). Universal distance modes from DESI BAO and Type Ia supernovae: What do cosmological rulers actually measure? arXiv:2606.30527. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.30527

item.title: 013 - When AI Makes Discoveries
item.description:
Highly Accurate Protein Structure Prediction with AlphaFold (July 2021) + Discovering Faster Matrix Multiplication Algorithms with Reinforcement Learning (October 2022) + Faster Sorting Algorithms Discovered Using Deep Reinforcement Learning (June 2023)
In this episode we unpack DeepMind's discovery trilogy: three open-access Nature papers in which the AlphaZero lineage stops playing board games and starts producing real discoveries. John Jumper, Demis Hassabis and colleagues deliver AlphaFold, the first computational method to predict protein structures at near-experimental accuracy; Alhussein Fawzi and colleagues follow with AlphaTensor, which finds faster matrix multiplication algorithms than any human has; and Daniel Mankowitz and colleagues close the arc with AlphaDev, whose machine-discovered sorting routines now run inside the C++ standard library. The shared thesis: recast a hard scientific or algorithmic search problem as a single-player game with a verifiable reward, and reinforcement learning can push past human intuition.
We walk through AlphaFold's blind-test dominance at CASP14 and the redesigned network that leverages multi-sequence alignments to reach atomic accuracy even without a known homologous structure; AlphaTensor's TensorGame, which frames matrix multiplication as low-rank tensor decomposition and yields a 4x4 finite-field algorithm beating Strassen's two-level construction for the first time in 50 years, plus hardware-tuned variants optimized for real runtime; and AlphaDev's AssemblyGame, which searches at the level of individual CPU instructions and produced fixed and variable small-sort routines fast enough to be merged into LLVM's libc++ sort. We close on the pattern that unites them - enormous action spaces, provable correctness as the reward, measured performance as the score - and on the open question of which discoveries this recipe can reach next.

item.title: 014 - The Internet Paradox Comes For AI Companions
item.description:
The Internet Paradox Comes For AI Companions (1998-2026)
In this episode we unpack a new Nature Human Behaviour study from Yutong Zhang, Dora Zhao, Jeffrey Hancock, Robert Kraut, and Diyi Yang of Stanford and Carnegie Mellon, published August 2026, on what AI companionship does to psychological well-being. The team surveyed 1,131 adult Character.AI users and, remarkably, analyzed 464,687 real chat messages donated by 237 of them. The core finding: heavier chatbot use overall tracks with higher well-being, but companionship-oriented use tracks with lower well-being, and the association is strongest for the most intense, most self-disclosing users with the smallest human networks.
We walk through the triangulated companionship measures (self-report, relationship descriptions, and GPT-4o-classified chat histories), the regression results behind the headline betas, and what the donated conversations actually contain, from emotional support to romantic roleplay to genuinely dark territory. We then set the result against its intellectual ancestors: Kraut's 1998 Internet Paradox study, which found the same troubling shape in the early internet and shares an author with this paper twenty-eight years later; De Freitas and colleagues' experiments showing AI companions relieve loneliness in the moment by making users feel heard; Guingrich and Graziano's finding that companion chatbot users perceive social health benefits; and the OpenAI and MIT Media Lab analysis of three million ChatGPT conversations showing affective use concentrates in a small population of heavy users. We close on the question the paper leaves open: substitution versus compensation, and what responsible companion design would even look like.

item.title: 015 - Who Gets The Dangerous Model First
item.description:
Who Gets The Dangerous Model First (2022-2026)
In this episode we unpack a 77 page working paper released through the NBER in August 2026 by Joshua S. Gans of the University of Toronto's Rotman School of Management, on how to regulate an AI model that finds security flaws. The motivating fact is real and very recent: pointed at the world's open source code, an unreleased frontier model surfaced 23,019 findings, 6,202 of them initially rated high or critical, with 90.6 per cent of a sampled subset later validated. The same class of capability had already been used offensively in what its developer called the first largely autonomous cyber espionage campaign. Policy has responded with two instruments that were never designed together: a voluntary thirty day head start for government evaluators under Executive Order 14409, and an unsettled patchwork of liability rules. Gans argues that the two cannot be chosen separately, and that staged access and liability are complements rather than substitutes.
We walk through the flaw contest at the heart of the model, where a defender and an adversary search the same hidden stock of vulnerabilities and every flaw leaves the pool either patched or exploited, and the winner independence property that collapses it into one contest played flaw by flaw. We cover why liability is a weak instrument once a model is public, with a pass through bounded below one half so that doubling the liability rate cuts the exploited share by less than half because the adversary simply searches harder too, and why an exclusive window changes that arithmetic completely: before release, the extra defensive effort liability buys goes uncontested. We get into the deadline effect, where defensive effort climbs through the window and reaches full contest intensity exactly at release by the same logic Mortensen found in job search and benefit exhaustion, and the resulting insight that headway is drawdown, so what matters is protection depth rather than elapsed days. We then set the paper against the work it builds on and argues with: Toby Shevlane's structured access, which named the practice of controlling who may use a model and turned release into a question of access rather than publication; Landolt and colleagues' Oracle's Gambit, which reaches a strikingly similar conclusion from game theory, showing defender welfare turns on the capability gap rather than the shared level, so that handing one model to both sides traps defenders in a Red Queen's race; Koh and Sanguanmoo's adaptive speed limits, the rival timing instrument that caps how fast a technology may scale; and Kapoor, Bommasani, Narayanan and co-authors' marginal risk framework for open foundation models, which pushes back hardest by arguing the evidence for added misuse risk is thinner than the debate assumes. We close on the three findings most likely to unsettle a policymaker: optimal evaluation windows are bounded, so greater danger cannot justify waiting indefinitely; the efficient liability rate is partial rather than full compensation, because defensive search burns real resources; and liability alone cannot make a developer pick the regulator's release date, which is precisely what leaves a distinct job for a timing mandate.

item.title: 016 - When Every Grant Proposal Sounds Alike
item.description:
When Every Grant Proposal Sounds Alike (2024–2026)
In this episode we unpack a new PNAS study published on 11 August 2026 by Yifan Qian, Zhe Wen, Alexander C. Furnas, Yue Bai, Erzhuo Shao and Dashun Wang of Northwestern University's Center for Science of Science and Innovation, and we set it against the fight that broke out the same week over whether any of this can be measured at all. The Northwestern team got hold of something researchers almost never see: the confidential NSF and NIH proposal submissions of two large US R1 universities from 2021 to 2025, funded, unfunded and pending alike, paired with the full public population of 57,000 NSF and 74,000 NIH awards. Their finding is that large language models are already inside the federal funding pipeline, and that the proposals leaning on them hardest are the ones that most closely resemble whatever the agency funded the year before.
We walk through how they know it: Liang et al.'s distributional detection framework, which estimates the fraction of LLM-modified sentences in an abstract by calibrating real pre-ChatGPT 2021 grant text against GPT-3.5-turbo-0125 rewrites of the same abstracts, and which shows adoption jumping from 2023 into a bimodal split between researchers who barely touch these tools and researchers who lean on them hard. We cover the central result, measured as SPECTER2 embedding distance to the previous year's funded work: within a single investigator compared against themselves, heavier LLM involvement means about five percentile points less distinctiveness at NSF and four at NIH, and a placebo in which an LLM rewrites 2021 abstracts without changing the science barely moves the needle, which suggests the convergence is substantive rather than cosmetic. We follow the agency split that makes the paper strange, with no relationship at NSF between LLM use and either funding success or later output, against a roughly four percentage point rise in NIH funding probability and five percent more publications that evaporates once you restrict to top five percent hit papers. Then we turn to the dispute: Kusumegi et al.'s Science paper reporting output gains of 23.7 to 89.3 percent for LLM adopters, the PNAS Comment from Thomas Renault, Antonin Bergeaud and Clément Bosquet arguing that dating adoption to the first detector hit mechanically manufactures that rise, and the original authors' August 2026 reply showing the artifact is real but too small to explain their result. We close on Hao, Xu, Li and Evans in Nature, whose 41.3 million paper study finds AI-augmented scientists publishing 3.02 times more and drawing 4.84 times more citations while the collective range of topics contracts, and on the exploration versus exploitation question this leaves for agencies that are supposed to be funding the risky work.

item.title: 017 - How Much Agent Is Your Agent
item.description:
How Much Agent Is Your Agent (1996–2026)
In this episode we unpack a paper published in Nature on 12 August 2026 by Atoosa Kasirzadeh of Carnegie Mellon University and Iason Gabriel of Google DeepMind, who argue that we are trying to regulate AI agents without any agreed way of saying how much of an agent a given system actually is. The phrase "AI agent" now covers a chess engine, a chatbot, a browser-driving assistant and a self-driving car, and governance frameworks that treat them as one category will either smother the harmless ones or wave the dangerous ones through. Their proposal is to stop asking whether something is an agent and start measuring how much of one it is, along four dimensions, and then to draw the result as that system's "agentic profile."
We walk through the four dimensions and the gradations that make them usable: autonomy from A.0, entirely dependent on its principal, to A.5, all tasks with no oversight at all, a scale lifted deliberately from the Society of Automotive Engineers' six levels of driving automation; efficacy built as a matrix rather than a line, crossing the degree of causal impact from observation-only to comprehensive against whether the environment is simulated, mediated or physical, with Klyubin, Polani and Nehaniv's empowerment measure offered as one way to quantify it; goal complexity from GC.0, no goal and therefore not an agent, to GC.5, where the system generates its own goal structures and interprets underspecified objectives, with METR's work on how long a task a model can reliably finish as the practical yardstick; and generality from a single speciality to a fully general system, built on Morris and colleagues' Levels of AGI. We then read out the four worked profiles that make the framework concrete, and they are not where intuition puts them: AlphaGo scores A.3, E.1, GC.2, G.1, more autonomous than people assume but sealed inside a board; standalone ChatGPT-3.5 lands at A.2, E.2, GC.3, G.3, broad but almost powerless on the world; Claude 3.5 Sonnet with tool use reaches A.3, E.3, GC.4, G.3, jumping three of four dimensions on scaffolding alone; and a Waymo vehicle sits at A.4, E.4, GC.4, G.2, the narrow one that can actually kill someone. That yields the paper's sharpest claim, that an agentic profile is a property of a deployment rather than a model, so adding tools, memory or reasoning to the same base system makes it a different agent, and leaves open the individuation question the authors cannot yet answer: when does one agent become another. We set this against Franklin and Graesser, who asked the original version of the question in 1996 and answered it with a hard binary, against the working definitions from Shavit and colleagues at OpenAI and the harm taxonomy from Chan and colleagues, and against the one source here that genuinely disagrees, Mitchell, Ghosh, Luccioni and Pistilli at Hugging Face, who argue that full autonomy should be ruled out entirely rather than graded. We close on what changes if regulators adopt profiles, and on the authors' own concession that no validated metric exists yet for any of the four dimensions.

item.title: 018 - When Scaling Laws Reach The Body
item.description:
When Scaling Laws Reach The Body (2020–2026)
In this episode we unpack SONIC, published in Science Robotics on 12 August 2026 by Zhengyi Luo, Ye Yuan, Tingwu Wang and twenty-five colleagues at NVIDIA, with Linxi "Jim" Fan and Yuke Zhu advising. The claim is that the recipe that built large language models finally works on a physical body. Humanoid controllers have stayed stubbornly small, often three-layer networks trained on a handful of GPUs for one task at a time, each new skill demanding its own hand-engineered reward. SONIC's argument is that the obstacle was never the hardware, it was the choice of training task: pick motion tracking, which takes dense frame-by-frame supervision straight from motion capture and needs no reward engineering at all, and the familiar curves come back. Performance rises steadily with model size, data and compute, and it rises most on motions the robot has never seen, which is to say that scale buys generalization rather than just fit.
We walk through the three scaling axes and what each one buys: networks from 1.2 million to 42 million parameters, data from 4 million to 100 million frames drawn from roughly 700 hours and 317,000 clips of motion capture, and compute from 2,000 to 21,000 GPU hours, 128 GPUs running for seven days at the top end, trained in Isaac Lab and deployed on a Unitree G1. The largest model reaches 99.6 percent success at 23.8mm mean per-joint error on held-out motion content, against 98.0 percent and 27.7mm for the smallest. Against rival trackers it takes 98.5, 99.2 and 97.2 percent on test-content, test-repetition and PHUMA, where BeyondMimic manages 82.0, 85.4 and 73.8 and Any2Track 61.6, 69.4 and 78.5, cutting tracking error 42 percent below BeyondMimic. The sharper result is against a specialist: OpenHomie, the open release of Ben and colleagues' HOMIE system, is a single-task locomotion controller built for exactly this job, and it survives 43.0 percent of runs where the generalist SONIC survives 98.5, holding near-total stability to about 4 metres per second where the specialist collapses past 2. On the physical robot, 124 motions transfer at 99.2 percent, with the feet the weak point at 53.7mm against 29.0 in simulation. We set this against Kaplan and colleagues' 2020 power laws, the source of the borrowed recipe, and ask whether three points on a log axis really earn the name; against Peng's AMP and Tessler's MaskedMimic, the adversarial and masked-inpainting lineage that tried to unify character control and, SONIC argues, runs into mode collapse exactly as the motion dataset grows large enough to scale on; and against the team's own ASAP, which closed the simulation-to-reality dynamics gap all of this depends on. We close on the real-time kinematic planner that replans every 100 milliseconds in under 5 milliseconds on a laptop, the universal token space that lets VR teleoperation, video, text, music and vision-language-action models drive one policy without retraining, and the question underneath the whole result: whether human motion capture is a foundation or a ceiling, since a robot that learns only from recorded human movement inherits only human movement, and motion capture cannot be scraped the way text can.

item.title: 019 - When Thinking Stops Being Words
item.description:
When Thinking Stops Being Words (2019–2026)
In this episode we unpack BDH-CQ, a reasoning model posted to arXiv on 10 August 2026 by Björn Engdahl, Adrian Kosowski, Jan Chorowski and colleagues at Pathway, with an independent audit by co-authors at Bielik AI and New York University. Its claim is not that it is the smartest system on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus. It is that a 150-million-parameter model reaches 29.5 percent pass@2 on the public ARC-AGI-1 evaluation set for about seven hundredths of a cent per task, breaking through the previously reported cost-accuracy Pareto frontier, and that it gets there without writing a single word of its reasoning down. We set that result against five papers that built the ideas underneath it: the architecture it runs on, the benchmark that defines what it is being measured for, and three rival attempts to move reasoning out of language.
We walk through how BDH-CQ works, with demonstrations updating a recurrent memory one at a time and the query then solved by iteration in a high-dimensional latent workspace, and through what the authors find when they probe it: a latent reasoning dial that lifts accuracy from 21 to 29.5 percent with no tokens emitted, a consistency gap where 77.92 percent test-pair accuracy on ConceptARC collapses to 59.38 percent once a task must be solved in full, generalization ladders where boundary propagation extrapolates perfectly while eight-item ordering falls to one correct output in twenty-four, and the striking finding that a single demonstration at the target complexity rescues most of those failures. We trace the lineage through Adrian Kosowski's Dragon Hatchling, the brain-inspired post-Transformer architecture BDH-CQ extends; through François Chollet's definition of intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency, which supplies this episode's sharpest question about a model trained on a curated pile of ARC-style data; through Coconut from FAIR at Meta and Jonas Geiping's recurrent-depth models, the two closest precedents for thinking in continuous space; and through Sapient Intelligence's Hierarchical Reasoning Model, which scores a higher 40.3 percent but has to train a solver for each puzzle at roughly two thousand times the cost per task. We close on whether cost per unit of reasoning is the axis that now matters, and on the authors' own honest limits: a proprietary training recipe, an untouched ARC-AGI-2, and a system that solves two of three test inputs without having truly induced the rule.

item.title: 020 - When AI Runs The Whole Experiment
item.description:
When AI Runs The Whole Experiment (2026)
In this episode we unpack two papers posted on the same day, 12 August 2026, that both claim to automate the research process itself, and a third that says they cannot. Spark-to-Paper, from Zhuoyang Qian, Biao Wu, Wenhao Wang and colleagues at Vast Intelligence Lab and the University of Technology Sydney, argues that end-to-end paper generation needs no dedicated agent platform at all: it can be thirteen composable skills running inside an ordinary coding assistant. Mechanist, from Mengru Wang, Junfeng Fang, Ningyu Zhang, Huajun Chen and collaborators at Zhejiang University, the National University of Singapore and UC San Diego, points the same idea at a harder target, using an agentic system as a scientific instrument to discover the mechanisms of AI intelligence. Against both, a large team led by Peter Kirgis and Sayash Kapoor with Arvind Narayanan, Helen Toner and Gillian Hadfield reports that when frontier agents were handed the central question of a real unpublished paper, the paper's own authors rejected the results outright.
We walk through Spark-to-Paper's separation of model judgment from deterministic gates, its Proposal and Data-Aware modes, and the ablation where fabrication detection climbs from 14 percent for a single-pass draft to 92 percent with the full integrity and adversarial-review stack, alongside 99.5 percent citation validity and the Self-Refutation Loop it names and caps at seven cycles. We turn to Mechanist's orchestrator and its hypothesis, experiment, verification and iteration agents, grounded in an interpretability knowledge graph of roughly 13,000 papers over a 43-million-paper cross-disciplinary base, and to what it actually found: that unsafe traits survive content filtering and transfer across modalities, driving unsafe answers on chemistry lab-safety questions to 48.6 percent, and that models hold World Knowledge, Personal Belief and Attributed Belief in separate attention heads making up about 0.05 percent of parameters. Then we set both against the shadow evaluations, where agents given six days and three thousand dollars of compute did all the engineering unaided and still scored 2 out of 6 and 1 out of 6 from confident expert reviewers, failing on judgment, budget awareness, backtracking and instruction drift. We close on the question underneath all of it, live in Nature's own news pages this month: if a machine can produce a cleaner manuscript than we do and surface a safety result nobody had noticed, but cannot tell whether the question was worth asking, what part of research have we actually automated?
